summary: Describes a Policy Information Base module for controlling how usage of policies is collected and reported by a device. It lets a policy decision point choose which policy objects count usage, what to count, and when to report. This RFC is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A device can keep count of how often each rule is used. This memo lets a controlling server pick what to count and when. It is now historic.

questions: what is a policy information base
how does policy usage feedback work
what are selection and usage policies
subtitle: How a policy server collects and reports device rule usage

tldr.problem: When policies (network rules) are installed on a device, administrators need visibility into which rules are actually being used and how often, but the device needs flexible control over what gets counted and reported.
tldr.mechanism: A Policy Information Base module defines how a policy-controlled device tracks usage of installed policies, links usage counters to the rules they measure, and reports them periodically or on demand to the policy server.
tldr.outcome: Policy servers can monitor real-world usage of their rules, detect unused policies, identify bottlenecks, and manage report intervals and thresholds, but the system was experimental and is now historic.

today: RFC 3571 is Informational and Historic. COPS-PR and its Policy Information Base framework did not become the standard for policy provisioning and monitoring. Modern network management uses different approaches such as NETCONF and YANG for device configuration and telemetry systems for collecting device metrics.

sections.title: Overview of Policy Feedback
sections.content:
RFC 3571 defines a Policy Information Base (PIB) module for policy usage feedback. A PIB is a set of data classes and objects that devices use to accept policy configuration from a policy server.

The framework builds on COPS-PR (Common Open Policy Service with Policy Provisioning), which allows a Policy Decision Point (PDP) to install policies on a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) in a device. This RFC defines how a device tracks the usage of installed policies (which rules are hit, how many packets matched, how many bytes were processed) and reports that information back to the policy server. The document is structured as a framework that other policy modules can extend for their specific technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: A policy server sends rules to a device. The device counts how often each rule is used. This memo defines the form in which the device reports those counts back to the server.

sections.title: Selection, Usage and Linkage Policies
sections.content:
The feedback framework defines three linked types of policies. A selection criteria policy installed by the policy server specifies which installed policies a device should monitor. The selection criteria may refer to specific policies, or it may reference a more general policy already used for enforcement that also works for specifying what to measure (such as a role-capability combination that identifies a set of interfaces).

A usage policy defines what attributes are recorded by the device: counts of packets dropped, bytes processed, or other counters specific to the rule. The PIB defines two generic usage classes: frwkFeedbackTraffic for general traffic counts and frwkFeedbackIfTraffic for per-interface traffic. The policy server chooses which usage class suits its needs.

A linkage policy (the frwkFeedbackLinkTable) connects a selection criteria instance to a usage instance, and specifies when to report the usage: the maximum reporting interval, whether to include the data only if it has changed since the last report, or whether to report only if a threshold is met. This linkage allows one selection criteria to be reused with multiple usage policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Selection says which rules to measure. Usage says what to count. Linkage ties them together and says when to report.

sections.title: Reporting and Control Operations
sections.content:
When a device connects to a policy server, it announces which usage and selection classes it supports. The server may send policies to enable monitoring. The device then reports usage periodically or unsolicited at regular intervals set by the server's Accounting Timer. The server can control reporting with a Feedback Action class:

suspendMonitoringAndReports stops both tracking and reporting. suspendReports stops reporting but keeps tracking (the device maintains counters silently). resume resumes reporting at the next interval. solicitReport asks for an immediate report of all usage. The server can apply an action to all policies or to a specific list. Conditions on reporting allow the device to omit unchanged data or data below a threshold, except when reporting due to connection loss or policy expiration, when all usage must be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can tell the device to start counting, stop reporting, or send the counts now. The device can be told to only report if the number changed or crossed a threshold.

sections.title: Usage Counters and Data Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines two textual conventions for usage data: Usage32 and Usage64, unsigned integers that count events and monotonically increase. Unlike SNMP counters, a Usage value is absolute (starts at zero) and provides meaningful information at a single point in time, since the initial state and the time of any reset should be available.

When a device suspends monitoring and then resumes, the Usage counters continue from where they left off. If a counter would exceed its maximum value, the RFC requires the smaller Usage32 type to reset to zero and signal the reset through a timestamp or other mechanism.

A Feedback Traffic instance contains packet and byte counts referencing a linkage instance. The Feedback Interface Traffic variant adds an interface index to associate counts with specific interfaces when a policy applies to multiple interfaces, allowing per-interface usage collection.
sections.plainLanguage: Usage counters track events, starting from zero. They go up when something happens. If you suspend counting, they remember where they left off.

sections.title: Policy Classes and Grouping
sections.content:
The framework PIB is organized into three logical groups. The Feedback Report Group contains classes for actions and reporting control: Feedback Action, Feedback Action List, Feedback Linkage, and Feedback Traffic Statistics Threshold. The Feedback Usage Group contains the two usage classes (Feedback Traffic and Feedback Interface Traffic) that define what counters are collected. The Feedback Selection Group contains a selection class for role-based filtering of interfaces.

A device may support multiple usage feedback classes: the server chooses which to link with each selection criterion. The framework also addresses under-specified selection criteria: if a selection policy refers to a template or object that is instantiated multiple times on the device, and no additional qualifiers are provided, the linkage may generate multiple usage instances, one for each instantiation. Qualifiers in the usage policy (such as an interface index) disambiguate which instance each counter belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework defines different classes for actions, counting, and selection. The server picks which classes to use and how to link them based on what it needs to measure.
